outcome: The infinitude of amicable pairs remains an open conjecture; nothing in the window settled it, moved it, or produced a directly relevant partial result. Only variant/generalization papers, a characterization of a restricted sub-family, a Lean formalization of pre-existing generation rules, and continued computational enumeration of known pairs were found.
summary: The question 'are there infinitely many amicable numbers/pairs?' is still listed as open by every current source checked: the live Wikipedia article on amicable numbers explicitly states 'It is unknown if there are infinitely many pairs of amicable numbers,' and Carl Pomerance's survey makes the same point. No paper found in the 26 January 2024–present window claims a proof, a disproof, or even a non-trivial partial advance on the infinitude question itself. What does exist in the window: (1) S. I. Dimitrov's 'Generalizations of amicable numbers' (arXiv:2408.07387, Aug 2024), which defines (α,β)-amicable pairs and conjectures (does not prove) infinitude for that generalized family — a related/variant problem under §3.1, not a case of the stated problem, since it changes the definition rather than restricting it; (2) an English translation of Euler's 1750 paper on amicable numbers (arXiv:2409.08783, Sept 2024) — historical, no new mathematics; (3) 'Amicable numbers and their connection to the Euler totient function' (arXiv:2512.22319, Dec 2025), a structural characterization of amicable pairs whose gcd is a power of two — a case restricted by a structural condition, but it proves an identity/characterization, not a fact about existence of infinitely many such pairs, so it does not bear on the infinitude question; (4) 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory' (arXiv:2601.07444), a Lean 4 formalization of the classical Thabit and Euler generation rules and the Borho-Hoffmann breeding method, plus computational search bounds beyond 10^65 for coprime pairs — this formalizes known generation methods, not a proof of infinitude, and uses only Lean's built-in tactics (zify, ring), not any AI system; (5) the Sergei Chernykh/BOINC 'Amicable Numbers' distributed-computing project, which has extended the exhaustive search of amicable pairs (smaller member below 10^18, with over a billion pairs known in total across informal counts, and an active search pushing toward 10^21) — per the explicit rule in §3.1, extending a search to a larger bound narrows where a counterexample to finiteness could hide but does not touch whether infinitely many pairs exist, so this is not a change to the problem. No AI system was found associated with any of this work; the Lean formalization uses only the proof assistant's built-in automation, which is explicitly excluded from the AI-involvement codes. I am satisfied nothing has escaped this search: I checked the live Wikipedia article, a leading survey (Pomerance), the OEIS wiki, the active BOINC project's own site, and the arXiv listing for amicable-number papers 2024–2025, and every substantive hit either predates the window, is a variant/generalization, or is a computational extension that the stated rules exclude from counting.
competing_reading: One could argue the (α,β)-amicable generalization (Dimitrov 2024) is 'a case' rather than 'a variant' if the ordinary amicable pairs are recovered at α=β=1, making the classical conjecture a special case of Dimitrov's Conjecture 6. But Dimitrov's paper only conjectures infinitude for the generalized family; it does not prove anything, so even under that reading there is no settled result to record — the classification as 'no change' is unaffected either way.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude for the classical (1,1) amicable pairs specifically (not a generalized family), or a paper explicitly stating it resolves the classical conjecture, would settle the ambiguity and change the status away from open.
